answer: Justifying faith is a saving grace, wrought in the heart of a sinner by the Spirit and word of God, whereby he, being convinced of his sin and misery, and of the disability in himself and all other creatures to recover him out of his lost condition, not only assenteth to the truth of the promise of the gospel, but receiveth and resteth upon Christ and his righteousness, therein held forth, for pardon of sin, and for the accepting and accounting of his person righteous in the sight of God for salvation.
right_choice: Saving grace wrought by Spirit and word; conviction of sin and misery; receiving and resting on Christ and his righteousness for pardon
wrong_choices: Divine grace wrought by the Spirit alone; rejection of sin; believing in Christ's person and work for salvation. | Transforming grace wrought by sacraments and preaching; repentance from sin; personal effort combined with Christ for pardon. | Intellectual assent to the gospel wrought by the word; understanding of sin; acceptance of Christian doctrine for salvation.
verses: Ephesians 1:13; John 1:12; Philippians 3:9; Acts 10:43; Acts 2:37; Ephesians 2:1
basis_note: No single verse gives the full definition, but together they teach it: hearing and believing the gospel by the Spirit (Eph 1:13), receiving Christ for forgiveness and righteousness (John 1:12, Phil 3:9, Acts 10:43), convicted of sin (Acts 2:37), and dead in sins (Eph 2:1).

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: How does faith justify a sinner in the sight of God?
answer: Faith justifies a sinner in the sight of God, not because of the other graces that always accompany it, or because of good works that are its fruits, nor because the grace of faith or any act of it is credited to him for his justification; but only because it is the instrument by which he receives and applies Christ and His righteousness.
right_choice: Faith justifies not as good works or faith itself imputed, but as instrument to receive and apply Christ's righteousness
wrong_choices: Good works justify through faith, with faith itself the instrument God uses to impute Christ's obedience. | Faith justifies because believers receive Christ and apply their own righteousness through the power of the Holy Spirit. | Faith justifies because it is itself the gift of God's righteousness imputed and accounted to believers for salvation.
reference: Gal 3:11; Rom 3:28; Rom 4:5; Rom 10:10; John 1:12; Phil 3:9; Gal 2:16
basis_note: Paul rejects a righteousness from the law and receives the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ, justified by faith apart from works. The word "instrument" is the catechism's own summary of this.
doubt: Romans 4:5 says faith itself "is credited as righteousness," which sits uneasily with the answer's denial that the act of faith is credited, so the answer reads "faith" there as the means of receiving Christ.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The catechism's teaching and all three wrong choices remain correctly wrong under the listed verses, but the wording used archaic KJV terms ('doth', 'receiveth', 'thereof') out of step with the site's BSB style, so it was reworded into modern English without changing its meaning.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is adoption?
answer: Adoption is an act of the free grace of God, in and for his only Son Jesus Christ, whereby all those that are justified are received into the number of his children, have his name put upon them, the Spirit of his Son given to them, are under his fatherly care and dispensations, admitted to all the liberties and privileges of the sons of God, made heirs of all the promises, and fellow heirs with Christ in glory.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is sanctification?
answer: Sanctification is a work of God's grace, whereby they whom God hath, before the foundation of the world, chosen to be holy, are in time, through the powerful operation of his Spirit applying the death and resurrection of Christ unto them, renewed in their whole man after the image of God; having the seeds of repentance unto life, and all other saving graces, put into their hearts, and those graces so stirred up, increased, and strengthened, as that they more and more die unto sin, and rise unto newness of life.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is repentance unto life?
answer: Repentance unto life is a saving grace, wrought in the heart of a sinner by the Spirit and word of God, whereby, out of the sight and sense, not only of the danger, but also of the filthiness and odiousness of his sins, and upon the apprehension of God's mercy in Christ to such as are penitent, he so grieves for and hates his sins, as that he turns from them all to God, purposing and endeavoring constantly to walk with him in all the ways of new obedience.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Wherein do justification and sanctification differ?
answer: Although sanctification be inseparably joined with justification, yet they differ, in that God in justification imputeth the righteousness of Christ; in sanctification his Spirit infuseth grace, and enableth to the exercise thereof; in the former, sin is pardoned; in the other, it is subdued: the one doth equally free all believers from the revenging wrath of God, and that perfectly in this life, that they never fall into condemnation; the other is neither equal in all, nor in this life perfect in any, but growing up to perfection.
right_choice: Justification imputes Christ's righteousness, pardons sin, perfectly frees from wrath; sanctification infuses grace, subdues sin, grows but never perfect
wrong_choices: Justification and sanctification both impute righteousness, both completely free from sin, both perfect in this life for believers. | Justification frees from guilt; sanctification removes sinful nature completely; both are unequal in believers and never finished. | Justification pardons sin gradually through faith; sanctification immediately frees from wrath and infuses perfect holiness eternally.
verses: Romans 4:6-8; Romans 8:33-34; Romans 6:6; Romans 6:14; Ezekiel 36:27; Philippians 3:12-14; 1 John 1:8
basis_note: Romans 4:6-8 says God credits righteousness apart from works and does not count sin, while Ezekiel 36:27 has God's Spirit enabling obedience. Philippians 3:12-14 and 1 John 1:8 show believers not yet perfect here.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Whence ariseth the imperfection of sanctification in believers?
answer: The imperfection of sanctification in believers ariseth from the remnants of sin abiding in every part of them, and the perpetual lustings of the flesh against the spirit; whereby they are often foiled with temptations, and fall into many sins, are hindered in all their spiritual services, and their best works are imperfect and defiled in the sight of God.
right_choice: Remnants of sin and flesh's lusts against spirit cause temptations, sins, hindered services, and imperfect works before God
wrong_choices: The best works of believers are perfect before God once they have truly been justified | Sanctification is imperfect in some believers who fail to exercise proper faith and obedience to God's law | The imperfection of sanctification arises from external temptations of the world, not from sin remaining in believers
basis_note: Paul says nothing good lives in his flesh and that another law wars in his body against the law of his mind, so sin remaining in the believer is the source of the imperfection.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Can true believers, despite their imperfections, temptations and sins, totally or finally fall away from the state of grace?
answer: No. True believers, by reason of the unchangeable love of God, and his decree and covenant to give them perseverance, their inseparable union with Christ, his continual intercession for them, and the Spirit and seed of God abiding in them, can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.
right_choice: No, they are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation
wrong_choices: Yes, God's love lasts only as long as their own faithfulness lasts | Yes, they fall away whenever their good works fail | Yes, any serious sin or temptation can finally separate them from grace
basis_note: Christ's sheep "will never perish" and no one can snatch them from His hand; God promises never to turn away from doing good to them, and believers are shielded by God's power through faith.
audit_why: The negative question made "True" confusing, since the catechism's answer is "No", and it had only one wrong choice, so I reworded the question and gave it three wrong choices that the catechism's teaching rules out.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Can true believers be infallibly assured that they are in the estate of grace, and that they shall persevere therein unto salvation?
answer: Such as truly believe in Christ, and endeavor to walk in all good conscience before him, may, without extraordinary revelation, by faith grounded upon the truth of God's promises, and by the Spirit enabling them to discern in themselves those graces to which the promises of life are made, and bearing witness with their spirits that they are the children of God, be infallibly assured that they are in the estate of grace, and shall persevere therein unto salvation.
right_choice: True believers may be infallibly assured by faith grounded in God's promises and the Spirit's witness with their spirits.
wrong_choices: They may hope and expect assurance but cannot have certainty without an extraordinary revelation from God. | Assurance is the essence of faith itself, so all true believers possess full assurance always. | Only the church leaders through their spiritual discernment can assure believers of their salvation state.
basis_note: John wrote so that believers may know they have eternal life (1 John 5:13). The Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are God's children (Romans 8:16), and Hebrews 6:11 urges diligence to make hope sure.
audit_why: The catechism's teaching and the wrong choices were sound, but the right choice was too long, so I shortened it and kept the word "infallibly".

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Are all true believers at all times assured of their present being in the estate of grace, and that they shall be saved?
answer: Assurance of grace and salvation not being of the essence of faith, true believers may wait long before they obtain it; and, after the enjoyment thereof, may have it weakened and intermitted, through manifold distempers, sins, temptations, and desertions; yet are they never left without such a presence and support of the Spirit of God as keeps them from sinking into utter despair.
right_choice: True believers may lack assurance long or lose it through temptations, but the Spirit prevents them from sinking into despair.
wrong_choices: Yes. All true believers always maintain full assurance of their salvation and never experience doubt. | Those who lose assurance were never truly believers, for real faith brings constant certainty. | No. True believers are never assured of their salvation but must always hope and fear.
basis_note: Psalm 88 shows a believer in despair and God seemingly rejecting him, and Isaiah 54 says God forsook His people for a moment, yet His loving devotion will not depart. Psalm 73:23 adds that God is always with them.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the communion in glory which the members of the invisible church have with Christ?
answer: The communion in glory which the members of the invisible church have with Christ, is in this life, immediately after death, and at last perfected at the resurrection and day of judgment.
right_choice: Communion in glory in this life, immediately after death, and perfected at resurrection and day of judgment
wrong_choices: The communion in glory of the invisible church is the same as the visible church's communion in Christ | The communion in glory is only after death and is not experienced in any way before the resurrection | Communion in glory is imperfect in this life and remains imperfect even after the resurrection
basis_note: Believers are being transformed into Christ's image now (2 Cor 3:18), will be with Him in Paradise the day they die (Luke 23:43), and will always be with the Lord at His coming (1 Thess 4:17).

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the communion in glory with Christ which the members of the invisible church enjoy in this life?
answer: The members of the invisible church have communicated to them in this life the firstfruits of glory with Christ, as they are members of him their head, and so in him are interested in that glory which he is fully possessed of; and, as an earnest thereof, enjoy the sense of God's love, peace of conscience, joy in the Holy Spirit, and hope of glory; as, on the contrary, sense of God's revenging wrath, horror of conscience, and a fearful expectation of judgment, are to the wicked the beginning of their torments which they shall endure after death.
right_choice: Believers enjoy God's love, peace, joy, and hope as firstfruits of glory; the wicked, God's wrath and fear of judgment.
wrong_choices: Believers should feel afraid and doubtful now; the wicked alone enjoy peace and worldly pleasures in this life. | All experience equal joy and peace now; true distinction between saved and lost comes only after death and judgment. | The Spirit destroys conscience in believers so they never feel guilt; the wicked alone have inner torment.
verses: Ephesians 2:6; 2 Corinthians 1:22; Romans 5:5; Romans 5:1-2; Romans 14:17; Romans 2:8; Hebrews 10:27
basis_note: Believers are raised and seated with Christ (Eph 2:6), given the Spirit as a pledge (2 Cor 1:22), with God's love poured out and peace, joy in the Spirit, and hope of glory (Rom 5:1-5; 14:17). The wicked face wrath and fearful expectation of judgment (Rom 2:8; Heb 10:27).
audit_why: The answer used the old wording "Holy Ghost", so it now says "Holy Spirit" as the BSB does. The Mark 9:44 reference was dropped because that verse is not in the BSB text. The right choice was shortened by one word to fit the limit. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound, but the reference cited the wrong verses (Eph 2:5 and Rom 2:9, plus unrelated Gen 4:13 and Matt 27:4); it now points to the correct verses (Eph 2:6, 2 Cor 1:22, Rom 5:5, Rom 5:1-2, Rom 14:17, Rom 2:8, Heb 10:27) that actually hold this teaching.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Shall all men die?
answer: Death being threatened as the wages of sin, it is appointed unto all men once to die; for that all have sinned.
right_choice: Death as the wages of sin is appointed unto all men once, for all have sinned
wrong_choices: Death is appointed unto all men except those who escape through righteousness and good works | Death is the wage of sin appointed only to those who reject Christ and are unbelievers | All men will die once, but death is not truly the result of sin but of nature
basis_note: Romans 6:23 calls death the wages of sin, Hebrews 9:27 says man is appointed to die once, and Romans 5:12 says death passed to all men because all sinned.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Death, being the wages of sin, why are not the righteous delivered from death, seeing all their sins are forgiven in Christ?
answer: The righteous shall be delivered from death itself at the last day, and even in death are delivered from the sting and curse of it; so that, although they die, yet it is out of God's love, to free them perfectly from sin and misery, and to make them capable of further communion with Christ in glory, which they then enter upon.
right_choice: Righteous are freed from death's sting through God's love which frees them from sin and unites them with Christ in glory.
wrong_choices: Death remains their penalty for sin, which they must partly pay before they can enter glory. | Their sins are forgiven, but God's anger still strikes them in death until the last day. | They experience death like all unbelievers but with spiritual comfort and peace in their final moments.
basis_note: Death is the last enemy destroyed (1 Cor 15:26), and in death the sting is taken away by Christ's victory (1 Cor 15:55-57). The righteous are taken from evil into peace (Isa 57:1-2) and depart to be with Christ (Phil 1:23).
audit_why: Two wrong choices were so close to the catechism's own teaching that someone could fairly pick them, so they were replaced with choices that clearly contradict it (death as a penalty still owed, or God's anger in death). Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound and well supported by 1 Cor 15:26,55-57, Isa 57:1-2, and Phil 1:23, but the reference list included extra proof texts not needed to establish the answer, so it was trimmed to just those four confirmed verses.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the communion in glory with Christ, which the members of the invisible church enjoy immediately after death ?
answer: The communion in glory with Christ, which the members of the invisible church enjoy immediately after death, is, in that their souls are then made perfect in holiness, and received into the highest heavens, where they behold the face of God in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies, which even in death continue united to Christ, and rest in their graves as in their beds, till at the last day they be again united to their souls. Whereas the souls of the wicked are at their death cast into hell, where they remain in torments and utter darkness, and their bodies kept in their graves, as in their prisons, till the resurrection and judgment of the great day.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are we to believe concerning the resurrection?
answer: We are to believe, that at the last day there shall be a general resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust: when they that are then found alive shall in a moment be changed; and the selfsame bodies of the dead which were laid in the grave, being then again united to their souls forever, shall be raised up by the power of Christ. The bodies of the just, by the Spirit of Christ, and by virtue of his resurrection as their head, shall be raised in power, spiritual, incorruptible, and made like to his glorious body; and the bodies of the wicked shall be raised up in dishonor by him, as an offended judge.
right_choice: General resurrection of just and unjust; living changed in moment; bodies raised and united to souls; just in power and incorruption
wrong_choices: Resurrection of all people, the living transformed instantly, bodies and souls reunited forever, wicked raised in glory like the just. | General resurrection only of righteous believers; living are perfected in moment; bodies raised incorruptible and glorified. | Universal resurrection of just and unjust; living changed to spiritual bodies; all raised incorruptible in power.
basis_note: Acts 24:15 gives a resurrection of both righteous and wicked; 1 Corinthians 15:51-52 says the living are changed in an instant; John 5:28-29 says those in graves come out; 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 and Philippians 3:21 describe the glorified body.
audit_why: One wrong choice was almost the same as the catechism's teaching, so I changed its ending to say the wicked are raised in glory like the just, which the catechism clearly denies.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What shall immediately follow after the resurrection?
answer: Immediately after the resurrection shall follow the general and final judgment of angels and men; the day and hour whereof no man knows, that all may watch and pray, and be ever ready for the coming of the Lord.
right_choice: General and final judgment of angels and men; day and hour unknown, so all watch and pray
wrong_choices: Final judgment of mankind alone comes after resurrection; the day is known to the elect for their readiness. | The judgment precedes resurrection; both angels and men are judged; day and hour are foretold in Scripture. | The saints enter their rest without any judgment; the day and hour are known to the faithful who watch.
basis_note: John 5:28-29 places the resurrection of the dead alongside judgment; Jude 1:6 speaks of angels kept for judgment; Matthew 24:36, 44 and Luke 21:36 say the day is unknown, so watch and be ready.
audit_why: The third wrong choice actually stated the catechism's teaching of a final judgment of angels and men, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong choice, and the right choice was shortened to fit the length limit. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are sound, but the reference list given did not include John 5:28-29, the verse that actually ties the resurrection to the judgment that follows it; the reference is now corrected to the five verses that together hold the full answer.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What shall be done to the wicked at the day of judgment?
answer: At the day of judgment, the wicked shall be set on Christ's left hand, and, upon clear evidence, and full conviction of their own consciences, shall have the fearful but just sentence of condemnation pronounced against them; and thereupon shall be cast out from the favorable presence of God, and the glorious fellowship with Christ, his saints, and all his holy angels, into hell, to be punished with unspeakable torments, both of body and soul, with the devil and his angels forever.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What shall be done to the righteous at the day of judgment?
answer: At the day of judgment, the righteous, being caught up to Christ in the clouds, shall be set on his right, and there openly acknowledged and acquitted, shall join with him in the judging of reprobate angels and men, and shall be received into heaven, where they shall be fully and forever freed from all sin and misery; filled with inconceivable joys, made perfectly holy and happy both in body and soul, in the company of innumerable saints and holy angels, but especially in the immediate vision and fruition of God the Father, of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, to all eternity. And this is the perfect and full communion, which the members of the invisible church shall enjoy with Christ in glory, at the resurrection and day of judgment.
right_choice: Righteous caught to Christ's right, acquitted, judge reprobates, received to heaven, perfectly holy in God's presence eternally
wrong_choices: Righteous left on earth, tried again, judged by angels, purified in purgatory, then received to heaven with partial joy | Righteous set on Christ's left, pardoned, excluded from judging, received into an earthly kingdom, still liable to sin | Righteous raised in soul only, acquitted secretly, judged with the wicked, received into heaven, happy in soul but not body
basis_note: The righteous are caught up to meet the Lord, set at his right hand, acknowledged, given eternal life, made holy, joined by the saints and angels, and given rest and joy in God's presence.
audit_why: The three wrong choices described nearly the same blessings as the catechism's answer, so they were also right; I replaced them with choices that clearly contradict the teaching (left hand, purgatory, soul only, and so on). Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices carried the KJV phrase 'right hand'/'left hand' from Matthew 25:33, but the BSB text given for that verse says only 'on His right' and 'on His left,' so the wording was changed to match the BSB; the teaching itself, the wrong choices, and the reference were otherwise sound and are kept.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What did God at first reveal unto man as the rule of his obedience?
answer: The rule of obedience revealed to Adam in the estate of innocence, and to all mankind in him, besides a special command not to eat of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, was the moral law.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the moral law?
answer: The moral law is the declaration of the will of God to mankind, directing and binding everyone to personal, perfect, and perpetual conformity and obedience thereunto, in the frame and disposition of the whole man, soul and body, and in performance of all those duties of holiness and righteousness which he oweth to God and man: promising life upon the fulfilling, and threatening death upon the breach of it.
right_choice: God's declaration of will directing to personal, perfect, perpetual conformity and obedience in whole man, promising life and threatening death
wrong_choices: God's law requiring external obedience to commands and ceremonies; directing the believer's conduct; promising blessing for keeping it. | God's revelation of His nature and demanding personal obedience; binding all people to holiness; promising salvation and threatening judgment. | God's moral standard calling for perfect compliance in works and words; requiring inward assent and outer behavior of all.
basis_note: Moses declares God's statutes and ordinances to Israel (Deut 5:1), life comes to those who do them (Gal 3:12), a curse on those who break them (Gal 3:10), and holiness reaches soul and body (1 Thess 5:23) all the days of life (Luke 1:75).

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Is there any use of the moral law to man since the fall?
answer: Although no man, since the fall, can attain to righteousness and life by the moral law; yet there is great use thereof, as well common to all men, as peculiar either to the unregenerate, or the regenerate.
right_choice: No man can attain righteousness by law since fall, yet the law has great use for all and unregenerate and regenerate
wrong_choices: No man can be saved by the law; yet it has limited use only for unregenerate people. | Some men can attain righteousness through keeping the law; it serves the same purpose for all believers. | No person can perfectly obey the law after sin; it has particular use for the unregenerate only.
basis_note: Galatians 2:16 and Romans 3:20 show no one is justified by the law; 1 Timothy 1:8-9 says the law is good when used legitimately, and is laid down for the lawless. Romans 8:4 shows its righteous standard is fulfilled in believers.
audit_why: Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The catechism answer and choices are sound, but the reference list omitted Romans 3:20 and 1 Timothy 1:9 and cited Rom 8:3 instead of 8:4; the reference was corrected to Gal 2:16; Rom 3:20; 1 Tim 1:8-9; Rom 8:4, which together hold the answer.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Of what use is the moral law to all men?
answer: The moral law is of use to all men, to inform them of the holy nature and will of God, and of their duty, binding them to walk accordingly; to convince them of their disability to keep it, and of the sinful pollution of their nature, hearts, and lives; to humble them in the sense of their sin and misery, and thereby help them to a clearer sight of the need they have of Christ, and of the perfection of his obedience.
right_choice: Informs of God's will and duty, convinces of sin and inability, humbles us, and shows our need of Christ
wrong_choices: Informs of God's will and duty, and justifies those who obey it well enough to earn God's favor. | Informs of God's will, but frees the redeemed from any duty to walk by it. | Demonstrates God's justice and demands; convicts of transgression and weakness; promotes self-effort and moral improvement for salvation.
basis_note: God's holiness and will set the standard of duty (Lev 11:44). The law brings awareness of sin (Rom 3:20), all have fallen short (Rom 3:23), and the law cannot give life, so all are confined by sin and need faith in Christ (Gal 3:21-22).
audit_why: Two wrong choices described the law's use almost as the catechism does, so they could be picked fairly; they now contradict the catechism (earning favor by obedience, freedom from duty), and the right choice is shortened.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What particular use is there of the moral law to unregenerate men?
answer: The moral law is of use to unregenerate men, to awaken their consciences to flee from wrath to come, and to drive them to Christ; or, upon their continuance in the estate and way of sin, to leave them inexcusable, and under the curse thereof.
right_choice: Awakens consciences to flee wrath and drive to Christ; or if sin continues, leaves inexcusable and under curse
wrong_choices: Convinces unregenerate that they need more religious works and ceremonies to escape God's wrath | The moral law to unregenerate men shows them that perfect obedience is possible if they truly try | The law drives unregenerate to self-righteousness and trust in their own ability to keep it
basis_note: The law leads people to Christ (Gal 3:24), its accusing conscience (Rom 2:15), leaves men without excuse (Rom 1:20), and those who rely on works lie under its curse (Gal 3:10).

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What special use is there of the moral law to the regenerate?
answer: Although the regenerate, who believe in Christ, are delivered from the moral law as a covenant of works, so that they are neither justified nor condemned by it, it still has a special use for them: to show them how much they owe to Christ for fulfilling the law and bearing its curse in their place and for their good, and so to move them to greater thankfulness and to a more careful effort to obey it as the rule of their life.
right_choice: Regenerate delivered from law as covenant; law shows how bound to Christ for fulfilling it and enduring curse, provoking thankfulness
wrong_choices: Regenerate remain under law's covenant to maintain sanctification; law reminds of Christ's obedience and encourages obedience to it. | Believers are released from the law altogether; it has no further use, since Christ's grace replaces any rule of obedience. | Regenerate are freed from law's condemnation; law demonstrates their bondage to sin and need of continual grace.
basis_note: Believers are not under law but under grace (Rom 6:14), Christ bore the law's curse for us (Gal 3:13), the law's standard is fulfilled in us (Rom 8:3-4), and Christ redeemed us to be zealous for good works (Titus 2:14).
audit_why: One wrong choice said almost the same as the catechism's answer (freed from the law, yet grateful for Christ's work), so it was replaced with a clearly wrong one saying the law has no further use for believers. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and wrong choices are accurate against the four cited verses, but the reference list carried many extra proof-texts beyond what was needed to support this answer, so it was trimmed to just Romans 6:14; Galatians 3:13; Romans 8:3-4; Titus 2:14, which together clearly support it.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Where is the moral law summarily comprehended?
answer: The moral law is summarily comprehended in the ten commandments, which were delivered by the voice of God upon mount Sinai, and written by him in two tables of stone; and are recorded in the twentieth chapter of Exodus. The four first commandments containing our duty to God, and the other six our duty to man.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What rules are to be observed for the right understanding of the ten commandments?
answer: For the right understanding of the ten commandments, these rules are to be observed: 1. That the law is perfect, and binds everyone to full conformity in the whole man to its righteousness, and to entire obedience forever; so as to require the utmost perfection of every duty, and to forbid the least degree of every sin. 2. That it is spiritual, and so reaches the understanding, will, affections, and all other powers of the soul, as well as words, works, and gestures. 3. That one and the same thing, in different respects, is required or forbidden in several commandments. 4. That as, where a duty is commanded, the contrary sin is forbidden; and where a sin is forbidden, the contrary duty is commanded: so, where a promise is given, the contrary warning is included; and where a warning is given, the contrary promise is included. 5. That what God forbids is never to be done; what He commands is always our duty; yet not every particular duty is to be done at all times. 6. That under one sin or duty, all of the same kind are forbidden or commanded, together with all the causes, means, occasions, and appearances of it, and temptations to it. 7. That what is forbidden or commanded to ourselves, we are bound, according to our places, to try to see it avoided or performed by others, according to the duty of their places. 8. That in what is commanded to others, we are bound, according to our places and callings, to help them; and to take care not to share with others in what is forbidden them.
right_choice: The law is perfect binding to complete conformity, spiritual reaching all powers, with duties commanded and sins forbidden in commandments
wrong_choices: The law is a perfect guide requiring external conformity; it is rational and reaches the mind and will. | The law is absolutely binding to external obedience, concerning actions and words; it forbids gross transgressions only. | The law is perfect binding to reasonable effort, spiritual reaching the heart only, with each duty confined to one commandment
basis_note: The shown verses teach the law is perfect (Ps 19:7; James 2:10), spiritual and reaching inward sins (Rom 7:14; Matt 5:21-28), and that a sin's contrary duty is required (Eph 4:28; Lev 19:17). Rule 5 is not directly shown.
audit_why: One wrong choice said the law is perfect, spiritual and touches all of human nature, which is what the catechism teaches, so I replaced it with a choice that clearly contradicts the catechism. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The teaching and choices hold up well against the fuller set of verses, but the catechism's answer still used archaic KJV-style words ('bindeth,' 'unto,' 'thereof,' 'divers,' 'thereunto'), which were changed to modern wording as the site requires; the reference was tightened to the verses that actually hold the answer.

question: What special things are we to consider in the ten commandments?
answer: We are to consider, in the ten commandments, the preface, the substance of the commandments themselves, and several reasons annexed to some of them, the more to enforce them.
right_choice: Consider the preface, substance of the commandments, and reasons annexed to some to enforce them
wrong_choices: Only the preface and reasons of the Ten Commandments require consideration, not their substance | The substance of the commandments is the only thing to consider; the preface and reasons are less important | The commandments have no particular preface or annexed reasons, but stand as bare commands from God

question: What is the preface to the ten commandments?
answer: The preface to the ten commandments is contained in these words, I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Wherein God manifesteth his sovereignty, as being JEHOVAH, the eternal, immutable, and almighty God; having his being in and of himself, and giving being to all his words and works: and that he is a God in covenant, as with Israel of old, so with all his people; who, as he brought them out of their bondage in Egypt, so he delivers us from our spiritual thraldom; and that therefore we are bound to take him for our God alone, and to keep all his commandments.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the sum of the four commandments which contain our duty to God?
answer: The sum of the four commandments containing our duty to God is, to love the Lord our God with all our heart, and with all our soul, and with all our strength, and with all our mind.
right_choice: Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind
wrong_choices: Love your neighbor as yourself and do to others as you would want done to you | Offer sacrifices, keep the feasts, and worship only at the temple in Jerusalem | To fear God's wrath, obey his law, and trust only in his provision for our lives

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Which is the first commandment?
answer: The first commandment is, Thou shall have no other gods before me.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties required in the first commandment?
answer: The duties required in the first commandment are, the knowing and acknowledging of God to be the only true God, and our God; and to worship and glorify him accordingly, by thinking, meditating, remembering, highly esteeming, honoring, adoring, choosing, loving, desiring, fearing of him; believing him; trusting, hoping, delighting, rejoicing in him; being zealous for him; calling upon him, giving all praise and thanks, and yielding all obedience and submission to him with the whole man; being careful in all things to please him, and sorrowful when in anything he is offended; and walking humbly with him.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the first commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the first commandment are, atheism, in denying or not having a God; Idolatry, in having or worshiping more gods than one, or any with or instead of the true God; the not having and avouching him for God, and our God; the omission or neglect of anything due to him, required in this commandment; ignorance, forgetfulness, misapprehensions, false opinions, unworthy and wicked thoughts of him; bold and curious searching into his secrets; all profaneness, hatred of God; self-love, self-seeking, and all other inordinate and immoderate setting of our mind, will, or affections upon other things, and taking them off from him in whole or in part; vain credulity, unbelief, heresy, misbelief, distrust, despair, incorrigibleness, and insensibleness under judgments, hardness of heart, pride, presumption, carnal security, tempting of God; using unlawful means, and trusting in lawful means; carnal delights and joys; corrupt, blind, and indiscreet zeal; lukewarmness, and deadness in the things of God; estranging ourselves, and apostatizing from God; praying, or giving any religious worship, to saints, angels, or any other creatures; all compacts and consulting with the devil, and hearkening to his suggestions; making men the lords of our faith and conscience; slighting and despising God and his commands; resisting and grieving of his Spirit, discontent and impatience at his dispensations, charging him foolishly for the evils he inflicts on us; and ascribing the praise of any good we either are, have, or can do, to fortune, idols, ourselves, or any other creature.
right_choice: Atheism, idolatry, neglect of duty, ignorance, false thoughts of God, profaneness, hatred, self-love, unbelief, despair, pride, tempting God
wrong_choices: Covetousness, theft, murder, and adultery, which violate the commands about love of neighbor. | Disrespect to parents, false oaths, evil thoughts about neighbors, and failure to keep the Sabbath. | Lying, slander, bearing false witness, and harming a neighbor's good name.
verses: Psalms 14:1; Ephesians 2:12; Jeremiah 2:27-28; Acts 17:23; Acts 17:29; Isaiah 43:22-24; Hosea 4:6; Psalms 50:21; Galatians 5:20
basis_note: The shown verses condemn atheism (Ps 14:1), idolatry (Jer 2:27-28; Acts 17:23, 29), neglect and forgetfulness of God (Isa 43:22-24; Hos 4:6; Ps 50:21), and being without God (Eph 2:12); the full list is drawn from its proof texts.
audit_why: One wrong choice (false worship, witchcraft, neglect of prayer, self-righteousness) actually lists sins the catechism forbids in the first commandment, so I replaced it with sins against the ninth commandment, and I shortened the right choice to 20 words or fewer.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are we specially taught by these words before me in the first commandment?
answer: These words before me, or before my face, in the first commandment, teach us, that God, who seeth all things, taketh special notice of, and is much displeased with, the sin of having any other God: that so it may be an argument to dissuade from it, and to aggravate it as a most impudent provocation: as also to persuade us to do as in his sight,: Whatever we do in his service.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Which is the second commandment?
answer: The second commandment is, Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me; and shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties required in the second commandment?
answer: The duties required in the second commandment are, the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath instituted in his word; particularly prayer and thanksgiving in the name of Christ; the reading, preaching, and hearing of the word; the administration and receiving of the sacraments; church government and discipline; the ministry and maintenance thereof; religious fasting; swearing by the name of God, and vowing unto him: as also the disapproving, detesting, opposing, all false worship; and, according to each one's place and calling, removing it, and all monuments of idolatry.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the second commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the second commandment are, all devising, counseling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, any religious worship not instituted by God himself; tolerating a false religion; the making any representation of God, of all or of any of the three persons, either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness of any creature whatsoever; all worshiping of it, or God in it or by it; the making of any representation of feigned deities, and all worship of them, or service belonging to them; all superstitious devices, corrupting the worship of God, adding to it, or taking from it, whether invented and taken up of ourselves, or received by tradition from others, though under the title of antiquity, custom, devotion, good intent, or any other pretense whatsoever; simony; sacrilege; all neglect, contempt, hindering, and opposing the worship and ordinances which God hath appointed.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the reasons annexed to the second commandment, the more to enforce it?
answer: The reasons annexed to the second commandment, the more to enforce it, contained in these words, For I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me; and showing mercy unto thousands of them that love me, and keep my commandments; are, besides God's sovereignty over us, and propriety in us, his fervent zeal for his own worship, and his revengeful indignation against all false worship, as being a spiritual whoredom; accounting the breakers of this commandment such as hate him, and threatening to punish them unto divers generations; and esteeming the observers of it such as love him and keep his commandments, and promising mercy to them unto many generations.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is required in the third commandment?
answer: The third commandment requires, That the name of God, his titles, attributes, ordinances, the word, sacraments, prayer, oaths, vows, lots, his works, and whatsoever else there is whereby he makes himself known, be holily and reverently used in thought, meditation, word, and writing; by an holy profession, and Answerable conversation, to the glory of God, and the good of ourselves, and others.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the third commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the third commandment are, the not using of God's name as is required; and the abuse of it in an ignorant, vain, irreverent, profane, superstitious, or wicked mentioning, or otherwise using his titles, attributes, ordinances, or works, by blasphemy, perjury; all sinful cursings, oaths, vows, and lots; violating of our oaths and vows, if lawful; and fulfilling them, if of things unlawful; murmuring and quarreling at, curious prying into, and misapplying of God's decrees and providences; misinterpreting, misapplying, or any way perverting the word, or any part of it, to profane jests, curious or unprofitable Questions, vain janglings, or the maintaining of false doctrines; abusing it, the creatures, or anything contained under the name of God, to charms, or sinful lusts and practices; the maligning, scorning, reviling, or any wise opposing of God's truth, grace, and ways; making profession of religion in hypocrisy, or for sinister ends; being ashamed of it, or a shame to it, by unconformable, unwise, unfruitful, and offensive walking, or backsliding from it.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What reasons are annexed to the third commandment?
answer: The reasons annexed to the third commandment, in these words, The Lord thy God, and, For the Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain, are, because he is the Lord and our God, therefore his name is not to be profaned, or any way abused by us; especially because he will be so far from acquitting and sparing the transgressors of this commandment, as that he will not suffer them to escape his righteous judgment, albeit many such escape the censures and punishments of men.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is required in the fourth commandment?
answer: The fourth commandment requires of all men the sanctifying or keeping holy to God such set times as he hath appointed in his word, expressly one whole day in seven; which was the seventh from the beginning of the world to the resurrection of Christ, and the first day of the week ever since, and so to continue to the end of the world; which is the Christian sabbath, and in the New Testament called The Lord's day.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: How is the sabbath or the Lord's day to be sanctified?
answer: The sabbath or Lord's day is to be sanctified by an holy resting all the day, not only from such works as are at all times sinful, but even from such worldly employments and recreations as are on other days lawful; and making it our delight to spend the whole time (except so much of it as is to betaken up in works of necessity and mercy) in the public and private exercises of God's worship: and, to that end, we are to prepare our hearts, and with such foresight, diligence, and moderation, to dispose and seasonably dispatch our worldly business, that we may be the more free and fit for the duties of that day.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Why is the charge of keeping the sabbath more specially directed to governors of families, and other superiors?
answer: The charge of keeping the sabbath is more specially directed to governors of families, and other superiors, because they are bound not only to keep it themselves, but to see that it be observed by all those that are under their charge; and because they are prone ofttimes to hinder them by employments of their own.
right_choice: Directed to governors and superiors; they must keep it and ensure those under them observe it and not hinder them
wrong_choices: The sabbath is primarily for the common people; superiors need only ensure legal observance | The sabbath command applies equally to all people without any special charge to superiors and governors | Governors and superiors are exempt from keeping the sabbath so they can oversee their responsibilities
basis_note: Exodus 20:10 charges the head of the household that son, daughter, servants, livestock and the foreigner must not work on the Sabbath. Nehemiah 13:17 rebukes the nobles for profaning it, showing superiors' responsibility and their tendency to hinder others.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the fourth commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the fourth commandment are, all omissions of the duties required, all careless, negligent, and unprofitable performing of them, and being weary of them; all profaning the day by idleness, and doing that which is in itself sinful; and by all needless works, words, and thoughts, about our worldly employments and recreations.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the reasons annexed to the fourth commandment, the more to enforce it?
answer: The reasons annexed to the fourth commandment, the more to enforce it, are taken from the equity of it, God allowing us six days of seven for our own affairs, and reserving but one for himself, in these words, Six days shalt thou labor, and do all thy work: from God's challenging a special propriety in that day, The seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: from the example of God, who in six days made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: and from that blessing which God put upon that day, not only in sanctifying it to be a day for his service, but in ordaining it to be a means of blessing to us in our sanctifying it; Wherefore the Lord blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Why is the word Remember set in the beginning of the fourth commandment?
answer: The word Remember is set in the beginning of the fourth commandment, partly, because of the great benefit of remembering it, we being thereby helped in our preparation to keep it, and, in keeping it, better to keep all the rest of the commandments, and to continue a thankful remembrance of the two great benefits of creation and redemption, which contain a short abridgment of religion; and partly, because we are very ready to forget it, for that there is less light of nature for it, and yet it restraineth our natural liberty in things at other times lawful; that it comes but once in seven days, and many worldly businesses come between, and too often take off our minds from thinking of it, either to prepare for it, or to sanctify it; and that Satan with his instruments much labor to blot out the glory, and even the memory of it, to bring in all irreligion and impiety.
right_choice: Remembering helps us keep it and all the commandments, and we are very ready to forget it
wrong_choices: The word Remember is included to remind us that the Sabbath was created for human convenience and leisure | The word Remember shows that the Sabbath was a new law, first given at Sinai | Remembering the Sabbath means taking time for rest alone, without concern for spiritual worship or creation's significance
basis_note: The shown verses contain the word "Remember" (Exod 20:8) and tie remembrance to creation and redemption (Exod 20:11, Deut 5:15). The reasons about human forgetfulness, worldly business, and Satan's work are the divines' own reasoning, not stated in these verses.
audit_why: The catechism answer had a typo ("comesthbut"). The right choice was garbled and much longer than the others. The third wrong choice did not answer the question, so I replaced it with a believable wrong reason that Scripture contradicts (the Sabbath goes back to creation, Gen 2:2-3).

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the sum of the six commandments which contain our duty to man?
answer: The sum of the six commandments which contain our duty to man is, to love our neighbor as ourselves, and to do to others what we would have them to do to us.
right_choice: Love your neighbor as yourself, and do to others as you would have them do to you
wrong_choices: To rule over your neighbor wisely and ensure they fulfill their obligations to you | The sum of duty to man is to seek your own good first and help others when convenient | To maintain justice and equality by giving others what they earn through their own efforts
basis_note: Matthew 22:39 states "Love your neighbor as yourself," and Matthew 7:12 states "do to others as you would have them do to you," the two parts of the answer.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Which is the fifth commandment?
answer: The fifth commandment is, Honor thy father and thy mother; that thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Who are meant by father and mother in the fifth commandment?
answer: By father and mother, in the fifth commandment, are meant, not only natural parents, but all superiors in age and gifts; and especially such as, by God's ordinance, are over us in place of authority, whether in family, church, or commonwealth.
right_choice: Not only natural parents, but all superiors in age and gifts, especially those in authority in family, church, commonwealth
wrong_choices: Spiritual leaders and pastors exclusively, since the church is God's institution for directing believers' lives and growth | Political rulers and civic authorities alone, who govern the commonwealth and deserve honor as representatives of God | Only biological parents, since the commandment specifically uses the word 'father' and 'mother' literally in each case
basis_note: Paul tells Timothy to treat older men as fathers and older women as mothers, Elisha calls Elijah "my father," and Joseph is made a father to Pharaoh. "Father" reaches beyond natural parents to age, gifts, and authority.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Why are superiors styled Father and Mother?
answer: Superiors are styled Father and Mother, both to teach them in all duties toward their inferiors, like natural parents, to express love and tenderness to them, according to their several relations; and to work inferiors to a greater willingness and cheerfulness in performing their duties to their superiors, as to their parents.
right_choice: Styled Father and Mother to teach superiors to be like parents expressing love and tenderness, making inferiors more willing in duties
wrong_choices: Styled Father and Mother merely as traditional honorary titles honoring ancient custom, without implying loving care or concern | Called Father and Mother to reflect their absolute authority and power, similar to how strict parents govern children | Named Father and Mother because superiors must exercise firm discipline and correction over inferiors, like fathers discipline children
basis_note: Paul was gentle like a nursing mother and treated the Thessalonians as a father treats his children, and Naaman's servants called him "My father" and urged ready obedience.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the general scope of the fifth commandment?
answer: The general scope of the fifth commandment is, the performance of those duties which we mutually owe in our several relations, as inferiors, superiors, or equals.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the honor that inferiors owe to their superiors?
answer: The honor which inferiors owe to their superiors is, all due reverence in heart, word, and behavior; prayer and thanksgiving for them; imitation of their virtues and graces; willing obedience to their lawful commands and counsels; due submission to their corrections; fidelity to, defense and maintenance of their persons and authority, according to their several ranks, and the nature of their places; bearing with their infirmities, and covering them in love, that so they may be an honor to them and to their government.
right_choice: Due reverence in heart, word, and behavior; prayer and thanksgiving for them; willing obedience to their lawful commands
wrong_choices: Obedience to their commands, loving affection toward them as parents, and protection from all public criticism. | Respect shown only outwardly, submission only when it is forced upon them, and honor given only in public. | Prayer for their guidance, eager compliance with their every desire, and defense of their actions blindly.
verses: Romans 13:7; Hebrews 13:17; 1 Timothy 2:1-2; Philippians 3:17; 1 Samuel 26:15-16; 1 Peter 2:18
basis_note: Scripture teaches respect and honor to those owed it, obedience and submission to leaders, prayer for rulers, imitation of those who lead, defense of the king, and submission to masters. Together these match the listed duties.
audit_why: The marked right choice was about why superiors are called Father and Mother, not about the honor inferiors owe, so it now gives the catechism's actual list (reverence, prayer and thanksgiving, willing obedience). Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: One wrong choice ('submission to their lawful authority... without question') was too close to the catechism's real teaching and could be mistaken for the right answer, so it was replaced with a clearly wrong option (forced, only-public submission) of similar length and subject.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins of inferiors against their superiors?
answer: The sins of inferiors against their superiors are, all neglect of the duties required toward them; envying at, contempt of, and rebellion against, their persons and places, in their lawful counsels, commands, and corrections; cursing, mocking, and all such refractory and scandalous carriage, as proves a shame and dishonor to them and their government.
right_choice: Neglect of duties toward them; envy, contempt, and rebellion against them; cursing, mocking, and scandalous conduct that shames them and their government.
wrong_choices: Reverence in heart, word, and behavior; prayer and thanksgiving for them; and imitation of their virtues and graces. | Willing obedience to their lawful commands, due submission to their corrections, and defense of their persons and authority. | Bearing with their infirmities and covering them in love, so that they may be an honor to them.
basis_note: Neglecting parental honor and cursing parents (Matt 15:4-6), Joshua's jealousy (Num 11:28-29), contempt for Saul (1 Sam 10:27), rejecting God's king (1 Sam 8:7), mocking parents (Prov 30:17), and shameful conduct (Prov 19:26) together show the sins listed.
audit_why: The marked right choice described the duties inferiors owe, not their sins, and the wrong choices were also sins; the right choice now summarizes the catechism's list of sins, and the wrong choices now list the duties of honor. Rechecked against the verses that hold the answer: The answer and choices correctly reflect the Westminster Larger Catechism's teaching on the sins of inferiors (with the three wrong choices being the correct answer to the related 'honor' question, so they are clearly wrong here, not also right); only the reference needed trimming to the six verses confirmed to hold the answer.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is required of superiors towards their inferiors?
answer: It is required of superiors, according to that power they receive from God, and that relation wherein they stand, to love, pray for, and bless their inferiors; to instruct, counsel, and admonish them; countenancing, commending, and rewarding such as do well; and discountenancing, reproving, and chastising such as do ill; protecting, and providing for them all things necessary for soul and body: and by grave, wise, holy, and exemplary carriage, to procure glory to God, honor to themselves, and so to preserve that authority which God hath put upon them.
right_choice: Love, pray for, and instruct inferiors; reward the good, chasten the evil, provide for needs, and set holy examples.
wrong_choices: To rule with strict authority, maintain distance, and require absolute obedience without mercy or consideration. | To be friends with inferiors, share all authority equally, and let them do as they wish. | To demand perfection from inferiors and dismiss them harshly when they fail or make mistakes.
verses: Colossians 3:19; Ephesians 6:4; 1 Samuel 12:23; Romans 13:3-4; Job 29:12-17; 1 Timothy 5:8
basis_note: Scripture sets out these superior's duties across several passages: love and prayer (Col 3:19, 1 Sam 12:23), instruction (Eph 6:4), rewarding good and punishing evil (Rom 13:3-4), and protection and provision (Job 29:12-17, 1 Tim 5:8).

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins of superiors?
answer: The sins of superiors are, besides the neglect of the duties required of them, an inordinate seeking of themselves, their own glory, ease, profit, or pleasure; commanding things unlawful, or not in the power of inferiors to perform; counseling, encouraging, or favoring them in that which is evil; dissuading, discouraging, or discountenancing them in that which is good; correcting them unduly; careless exposing, or leaving them to wrong, temptation, and danger; provoking them to wrath; or any way dishonoring themselves, or lessening their authority, by an unjust, indiscreet, rigorous, or remiss behavior.
right_choice: Neglecting their duties, seeking their own glory and ease, commanding unlawful things, encouraging evil, discouraging good, and correcting unduly
wrong_choices: Disparaging the gifts of others, envying their good, and usurping a place above them | Disobeying lawful commands, resisting just correction, and murmuring against their counsels | Envying their superiors, despising their persons, and rebelling against their authority
basis_note: The shown verses condemn leaders who feed themselves and neglect their flock, seek their own glory and gain, give unjust or impossible orders, forbid good, provoke children, and fail to restrain wrong. The list follows from these proof texts.
audit_why: Two wrong choices described things the catechism also names as sins of superiors (rigorous or remiss behavior), and the right choice was too long, so I shortened it and replaced the wrong choices with the catechism's sins of inferiors and equals.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties of equals?
answer: The duties of equals are, to regard the dignity and worth of each other, in giving honor to go one before another; and to rejoice in each other's gifts and advancement, as their own.
right_choice: Regard each other's dignity and worth, give honor, and rejoice in each other's gifts and advancement
wrong_choices: To subordinate yourself to whichever equal seems most worthy at any given time | To maintain strict equality by never allowing anyone to receive greater honor or advancement | To compete with one another for recognition and to advance your own gifts above others
basis_note: Romans 12:10 calls believers to outdo one another in honor, Philippians 2:3 to count others more important, and Romans 12:15 to rejoice with those who rejoice, with Philippians 2:4 looking to others' interests.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins of equals?
answer: The sins of equals are, besides the neglect of the duties required, the undervaluing of the worth, envying the gifts, grieving at the advancement or prosperity one of another; and usurping preeminence one over another.
right_choice: Neglect of duties, undervaluing worth, envying gifts, grieving at advancement or prosperity, usurping preeminence
wrong_choices: Honoring one person more than others, preferring certain friendships above other relationships within the community | Celebrating others' success, acknowledging their talents, and supporting their advancement in various areas of life | Respecting authority figures and accepting their leadership role within the church and social structure
basis_note: Scripture shows the sins named: Miriam and Aaron dispute Moses' place, Galatians envy one another, Haman grieves at Mordecai's honor, and the disciples argue over who is greatest.
audit_why: The catechism says "advancement or prosperity", not "advancement of prosperity", so the answer and right choice were corrected to match; everything else was kept.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What is the reason annexed to the fifth commandment, the more to enforce it?
answer: The reason annexed to the fifth commandment, in these words, That thy days may be long upon the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee, is an express promise of long life and prosperity, as far as it shall serve for God's glory and their own good, to all such as keep this commandment.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties required in the sixth commandment?
answer: The duties required in the sixth commandment are, all careful studies, and lawful endeavors, to preserve the life of ourselves and others by resisting all thoughts and purposes, subduing all passions, and avoiding all occasions, temptations, and practices, which tend to the unjust taking away the life of any; by just defense thereof against violence, patient bearing of the hand of God, quietness of mind, cheerfulness of spirit; a sober use of meat, drink, physic, sleep, labor, and recreations; by charitable thoughts, love, compassion, meekness, gentleness, kindness; peaceable, mild and courteous speeches and behavior; forbearance, readiness to be reconciled, patient bearing and forgiving of injuries, and requiting good for evil; comforting and succoring the distressed, and protecting and defending the innocent.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the sixth commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the sixth commandment are, all taking away the life of ourselves, or of others, except in case of public justice, lawful war, or necessary defense; the neglecting or withdrawing the lawful and necessary means of preservation of life; sinful anger, hatred, envy, desire of revenge; all excessive passions, distracting cares; immoderate use of meat, drink, labor, and recreations; provoking words, oppression, quarreling, striking, wounding, and: Whatsoever else tends to the destruction of the life of any.
right_choice: Taking life except public justice, war, or defense; sinful anger, hatred, envy, revenge; immoderate use; provoking words; oppression; quarreling; striking
wrong_choices: Taking life is completely forbidden in all circumstances whatsoever, including lawful public justice, defensive warfare, and self-defense against attackers | Killing is prohibited except when motivated by personal anger and revenge, and when defending one's own honor and reputation | Murder is forbidden, but sinful anger toward wrongdoers, quarreling with rivals, harsh words, and striking in self-defense are permitted
basis_note: Scripture forbids unlawful killing (Gen 9:6; Num 35:31), anger and hatred (Matt 5:22; 1 John 3:15), neglecting the needy (James 2:15-16), anxious cares (Matt 6:31), harsh words, striking, drunkenness, and oppression.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties required in the seventh commandment?
answer: The duties required in the seventh commandment are, chastity in body, mind, affections, words, and behavior; and the preservation of it in ourselves and others; watchfulness over the eyes and all the senses; temperance, keeping of chaste company, modesty in apparel; marriage by those that have not the gift of continency, conjugal love, and cohabitation; diligent labor in our callings; shunning all occasions of uncleanness, and resisting temptations thereunto.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the seventh commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the seventh commandment, besides the neglect of the duties required, are, adultery, fornication, rape, incest, sodomy, and all unnatural lusts; all unclean imaginations, thoughts, purposes, and affections; all corrupt or filthy communications, or listening thereunto; wanton looks, impudent or light behavior, immodest apparel; prohibiting of lawful, and dispensing with unlawful marriages; allowing, tolerating, keeping of stews, and resorting to them; entangling vows of single life, undue delay of marriage; having more wives or husbands than one at the same time; unjust divorce, or desertion; idleness, gluttony, drunkenness, unchaste company; lascivious songs, books, pictures, dancings, stage plays; and all other provocations to, or acts of uncleanness, either in ourselves or others.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties required in the eighth commandment?
answer: The duties required in the eighth commandment are, truth, faithfulness, and justice in contracts and commerce between man and man; rendering to everyone his due; restitution of goods unlawfully detained from the right owners thereof; giving and lending freely, according to our abilities, and the necessities of others; moderation of our judgments, wills, and affections concerning worldly goods; a provident care and study to get, keep, use, and dispose these things which are necessary and convenient for the sustentation of our nature, and suitable to our condition; a lawful calling, and diligence in it; frugality; avoiding unnecessary lawsuits and suretyship, or other like engagements; and an endeavor, by all just and lawful means, to procure, preserve, and further the wealth and outward estate of others, as well as our own.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the eighth commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the eighth commandment, besides the neglect of the duties required, are, theft, robbery, man-stealing, and receiving anything that is stolen; fraudulent dealing, false weights and measures, removing land marks, injustice and unfaithfulness in contracts between man and man, or in matters of trust; oppression, extortion, usury, bribery, vexatious lawsuits, unjust enclosures and depopulations; engrossing commodities to enhance the price; unlawful callings, and all other unjust or sinful ways of taking or withholding from our neighbor what belongs to him, or of enriching ourselves; covetousness; inordinate prizing and affecting worldly goods; distrustful and distracting cares and studies in getting, keeping, and using them; envying at the prosperity of others; as likewise idleness, prodigality, wasteful gaming; and all other ways whereby we do unduly prejudice our own outward estate, and defrauding ourselves of the due use and comfort of that estate which God hath given us.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Which is the ninth commandment?
answer: The ninth commandment is, Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties required in the ninth commandment?
answer: The duties required in the ninth commandment are, the preserving and promoting of truth between man and man, and the good name of our neighbor, as well as our own; appearing and standing for the truth; and from the heart, sincerely, freely, clearly, and fully, speaking the truth, and only the truth, in matters of judgment and justice, and in all other things whatsoever; a charitable esteem of our neighbors; loving, desiring, and rejoicing in their good name; sorrowing for, and covering of their infirmities; freely acknowledging of their gifts and graces, defending their innocency; a ready receiving of a good report, and unwillingness to admit of an evil report, concerning them; discouraging talebearers, flatterers, and slanderers; love and care of our own good name, and defending it when need requireth; keeping of lawful promises; studying and practicing of whatsoever things are true, honest, lovely, and of good report.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the ninth commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the ninth commandment are, all prejudicing the truth, and the good name of our neighbors, as well as our own, especially in public judicature; giving false evidence, suborning false witnesses, wittingly appearing and pleading for an evil cause, outfacing and overbearing the truth; passing unjust sentence, calling evil good, and good evil; rewarding the wicked according to the work of the righteous, and the righteous according to the work of the wicked; forgery, concealing the truth, undue silence in a just cause, and holding our peace when iniquity calleth for either a reproof from ourselves, or complaint to others; speaking the truth unseasonably, or maliciously to a wrong end, or perverting it to a wrong meaning, or in doubtful and equivocal expressions, to the prejudice of truth or justice; speaking untruth, lying, slandering, backbiting, detracting, tale bearing, whispering, scoffing, reviling, rash, harsh, and partial censuring; misconstructing intentions, words, and actions; flattering, vainglorious boasting, thinking or speaking too highly or too meanly of ourselves or others; denying the gifts and graces of God; aggravating smaller faults; hiding, excusing, or extenuating of sins, when called to a free confession; unnecessary discovering of infirmities; raising false rumors, receiving and countenancing evil reports, and stopping our ears against just defense; evil suspicion; envying or grieving at the deserved credit of any, endeavoring or desiring to impair it, rejoicing in their disgrace and infamy; scornful contempt, fond admiration; breach of lawful promises; neglecting such things as are of good report, and practicing, or not avoiding ourselves, or not hindering: What we can in others, such things as procure an ill name.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Which is the tenth commandment?
answer: The tenth commandment is, Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbor's.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the duties required in the tenth commandment?
answer: The duties required in the tenth commandment are, such a full contentment with our own condition, and such a charitable frame of the whole soul toward our neighbor, as that all our inward motions and affections touching him, tend unto, and further all that good which is his.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the sins forbidden in the tenth commandment?
answer: The sins forbidden in the tenth commandment are, discontentment with our own estate; envying and grieving at the good of our neighbor, together with all inordinate motions and affections to anything that is his.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Is any man able perfectly to keep the commandments of God?
answer: No man is able, either of himself, or by any grace received in this life, perfectly to keep the commandments of God; but doth daily break them in thought, word, and deed.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: Are all transgressions of the law of God equally heinous in themselves, and in the sight of God?
answer: All transgressions of the law of God are not equally heinous; but some sins in themselves, and by reason of several aggravations, are more heinous in the sight of God than others.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are those aggravations that make some sins more heinous than others?
answer: Sins receive their aggravations, 1. From the persons offending: if they be of riper age, greater experience or grace, eminent for profession, gifts, place, office, guides to others, and whose example is likely to be followed by others. 2. From the parties offended: if immediately against God, his attributes, and worship; against Christ, and his grace; the Holy Spirit, his witness, and workings; against superiors, men of eminency, and such as we stand especially related and engaged unto; against any of the saints, particularly weak brethren, the souls of them, or any other, and the common good of all or many. 3. From the nature and quality of the offense: if it be against the express letter of the law, break many commandments, contain in it many sins: if not only conceived in the heart, but breaks forth in words and actions, scandalize others, and admit of no reparation: if against means, mercies, judgments, light of nature, conviction of conscience, public or private admonition, censures of the church, civil punishments; and our prayers, purposes, promises, vows, covenants, and engagements to God or men: if done deliberately, wilfully, presumptuously, impudently, boastingly, maliciously, frequently, obstinately, with delight, continuance, or relapsing after repentance. 4. From circumstances of time and place: if on the Lord's day, or other times of divine worship; or immediately before or after these, or other helps to prevent or remedy such miscarriages: if in public, or in the presence of others, who are thereby likely to be provoked or defiled.
right_choice: From the persons offending, parties offended, nature of offense, and circumstances of time and place
wrong_choices: From the sinner's knowledge, position, and power; offense against superiors; and public commission | From breaking express law, offense against the innocent, violation of sacred time, and malice | From the sinner's deliberate intent and resistance to correction, scandal caused, and persistence
basis_note: Luke 12:47-48 ties greater guilt to knowledge and entrusted position; Hebrews 10:29 to sins against Christ and the Spirit; 1 Corinthians 8:12 to wounding brethren; Numbers 15:30 to defiant sin; 2 Samuel 16:22 to sin done before all Israel.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What doth every sin deserve at the hands of God?
answer: Every sin, even the least, being against the sovereignty, goodness, and holiness of God, and against his righteous law, deserveth his wrath and curse, both in this life, and that which is to come; and cannot be expiated but by the blood of Christ.

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What doth God require of us, that we may escape his wrath and curse due to us by reason of the transgression of the law?
answer: That we may escape the wrath and curse of God due to us by reason of the transgression of the law, he requireth of us repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ, and the diligent use of the outward means whereby Christ communicates to us the benefits of his mediation.
reference: Acts.16.30-Acts.16.31; Acts.20.21; Matt.3.7-Matt.3.8; Luke.13.3,Luke.13.5; John.3.16,John.3.18; Prov.2.1-Prov.2.5; Prov.8.33-Prov.8.36

collection: Westminster Larger Catechism
question: What are the outward means whereby Christ communicates to us the benefits of his mediation?
